title: President Marcos: China’s playing of ‘Anak’ a ‘gracious’ gesture
summary: While the use of Freddie Aguilar’s classic hit “Anak” as musical accompaniment during his entrance to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gala dinner last Wednesday sparked…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — While the use of Freddie Aguilar’s classic hit “Anak” as musical accompaniment during his entrance to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gala dinner last Wednesday sparked online debate, President Marcos described it as a “very gracious choice” by the Chinese.

A Chinese orchestra played “Anak” as Marcos and First Lady Liza Marcos entered the hall for the APEC dinner in Shenzhen last Thursday, before they greeted Chinese President Xi Jinping and First Lady Peng Liyuan.
In an interview in China on Friday, Marcos said the song was played during his entrance, while “Leron Leron Sinta” was also played during the dinner.

“I thought their choice of that song was again a very, very warm gesture from the Chinese to, I guess, just make you feel at home and understand that they are thinking of how to express their comity and friendship,” Marcos said.
The use of “Anak,” a song about a repentant son, prompted online discussions about whether its lyrics carried an implied message about the territorial disputes between the Philippines and China.
Some questioned whether the song’s theme was an appropriate representation of Marcos and the country.
Marcos dismissed the speculation, saying the Chinese were simply playing popular music for their guests, similar to how the Philippines welcomes foreign dignitaries with familiar songs.
“I think you’re reading too much into it. They were just playing a song for their guests, the same way that we play popular songs in our country for our guests,” he said.
Presidential Communications Office Secretary Lino Cayetano, who accompanied Marcos to China, said “Anak” was also played during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations ceremonies in Manila.

“We played it too, because some people already knew it. That is why it was a very nice choice for the Chinese to make. They chose it because it is not only famous in the Philippines but also in many other countries,” Marcos said.
“Anak,” which means “child,” was a major hit in the Philippines in the 1970s before becoming an international success. The song has been translated into 51 languages.
